Spurious
spū´rĭ-ŭs
adj. (not genuine; counterfeit; of illegitimate birth)
Latin spurius, of illegitimate birth. The two senses meet in Hebrews 12:8, where those without chastening are called bastards, and not sons — a spurious sonship.

Biblical Definition

A spurious thing has the form without the descent. Hebrews applies it to sonship: if ye be without chastisement, “whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons” (Heb 12:8). Paul guards against forged letters: be not shaken “by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us” (2Th 2:2), and supplies a mark of authenticity: “The salutation of Paul with mine own hand, which is the token in every epistle: so I write” (2Th 3:17); “ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand” (Gal 6:11). And Peter warns that the counterfeit will arise from within: “there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies” (2Pe 2:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines spurious as not genuine; false; adulterate; not proceeding from the true source; and, of birth, not legitimate; bastard.

expand to see more

SPURIOUS, a. Not genuine; not proceeding from the true source, or from the source pretended; counterfeit; false; adulterate.

Spurious writings are such as are not composed by the authors to whom they are ascribed.

2. Not legitimate; bastard; as spurious issue.

Key Scripture

Heb 12:8 — "But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons."

2Th 2:2 — "That ye be not soon shaken in mind, or be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us, as that the day of Christ is at hand."

2Th 3:17 — "The salutation of Paul with mine own hand, which is the token in every epistle: so I write."

Gal 6:11 — "Ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand."

2Pe 2:1 — "But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction."

Modern Corruption

The test of genuineness is sought in feeling or profession, and Hebrews points to chastening.

expand to see more

Hebrews 12:8 is one of the most consoling verses in Scripture for anyone under God's discipline, and it is almost never read that way. The argument runs backwards from what everyone assumes: the son who is chastened is proved a son, and the man who never is has reason for concern. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not? Discipline is presented as the evidence of legitimacy, which turns a believer's hardest seasons into an argument for his standing rather than against it.

The other sense of the word bears on the canon, and Paul's practice is instructive. He assumed forged letters would circulate under his name — 2 Thessalonians 2:2 shows one had already unsettled that church — and his answer was not anxiety but a mark: the salutation in his own hand, the token in every epistle. The early church applied the same instinct on a larger scale, and the books it received were the ones with apostolic descent, which is what a canon is. The Reformation's appeal to Scripture depends on that discrimination having been made carefully, and it was.

Second Peter 2:1 is the reminder that counterfeits are an inside problem: false teachers among you, bringing in heresies privily. The spurious thing rarely announces itself as a rival; it presents as the genuine article with better credentials, and it establishes itself inside a congregation's trust before anyone examines its parentage. The remedy in both senses of the word is the same test: descent. Where did this come from? A doctrine, like a letter and like a son, is authenticated by its origin.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek nothos (G3541), illegitimate, a bastard; huios (G5207), son; semeion (G4592), a token, sign; pseudodidaskalos (G5572), a false teacher.

expand to see more

Greek nothos (G3541) — illegitimate, bastard; Hebrews 12:8 only.

Greek semeion (G4592) — token, mark; 2 Thessalonians 3:17 — the token in every epistle.

Greek pseudodidaskaloi (G5572) — false teachers; 2 Peter 2:1 only.

Usage

"“Then are ye bastards, and not sons” — and the chastened one is the son."

"“Nor by letter as from us” — forgeries were already circulating."

"“False teachers among you… privily” — it is an inside problem."
